authoredSolutions.15: By Hooke's law \(T=k(L-L_0)\): \(T_1=k(L_1-L_0)\) and \(T_2=k(L_2-L_0)\). Eliminating \(k\), \(T_1(L_2-L_0)=T_2(L_1-L_0)\), which gives the natural length \(L_0=\dfrac{T_2L_1-T_1L_2}{T_2-T_1}\). Hence option (D). [Source key (A) is incorrect — verified by the test case \(T_1{=}L_1{=}2,\ T_2{=}L_2{=}4\Rightarrow L_0{=}0\).]
authoredSolutions.25: Ruhemann's purple, the violet product of the ninhydrin test, exists as a resonance-stabilised anion; the structures shown in (a) and (c) are equivalent resonance contributors of the same species. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.26: An ester reacts with two equivalents of a Grignard reagent — the first gives a ketone, the second adds to it. Ethyl ethanoate \(CH_3COOC_2H_5\) with \(2\,CH_3MgBr\) gives \((CH_3)_3COH\) (2-methylpropan-2-ol). So 2 equivalents are needed. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.30: In \(I_3^-\) the central iodine has 5 electron domains (\(sp^3d\)): 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs, giving a linear ion. So there are 3 lone pairs on the central atom. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.35: A carbocation is resonance-stabilised when the positive charge sits next to a \(\pi\) bond or lone pair (allylic/benzylic), allowing the charge to delocalise. The cation in option (B) has such an adjacent \(\pi\) system. Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.40: Cold dilute \(KMnO_4\) (Baeyer's reagent) syn-hydroxylates the double bond of cyclohexene to the vicinal diol A, cyclohexane-1,2-diol. Hot acidic \(KMnO_4\) cleaves the double bond oxidatively, opening the ring to the diacid B, hexane-1,6-dioic acid (adipic acid). Hence option (A).
authoredSolutions.42: \((p\land\sim q)\Rightarrow(q\lor\sim p)\) is false only when \(p\land\sim q\) is true (\(p{=}T,q{=}F\)), where the consequent \(q\lor\sim p=F\). That is exactly when \(p\Rightarrow q\) is false, so the expression equals \(\sim(p\land\sim q)=p\Rightarrow q\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.43: \(e^{x-[x]}\) has period 1 with \(\int_0^1 e^x dx=e-1\). Writing \(a=10+f\), \(\int_0^a=10(e-1)+(e^f-1)=10e-11+e^f\). Setting this equal to \(10e-9\) gives \(e^f=2\), so \(f=\ln 2\) and \(a=10+\log_e 2\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.44: All six sum to \(39\), so the two unknowns sum to \(21\). Variance \(10.25\) gives \(\sum x^2=6(10.25+6.5^2)=315\); the known four contribute \(94\), so the two contribute \(221\). With \(x+y=21,\ x^2+y^2=221\Rightarrow xy=110\), so \(x,y\) are roots of \(t^2-21t+110=0\), i.e. 10 and 11. Hence option (A).
authoredSolutions.45: Since \((\sqrt{1-x}+\sqrt{1+x})^2=2+2\sqrt{1-x^2}\), the integrand is \(\tfrac12\ln 2+\tfrac12\ln(1+\sqrt{1-x^2})\). Integrating this even function over \([-1,1]\) (with \(x=\sin\theta\)) gives \(2\log_e 2+\tfrac{\pi}{4}-1\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.46: \(|\alpha|^2=\alpha\beta=\sqrt3\) so \(|\alpha|=3^{1/4}\); with \(\alpha+\beta=-3^{1/4}\), \(\mathrm{Re}(\alpha)=-\tfrac12 3^{1/4}\), giving \(\alpha=3^{1/4}e^{\pm i2\pi/3}\). Then \(\alpha^{12}=3^3=27\) and \(\alpha^{96}=3^{24}\), so \(\alpha^{96}(\alpha^{12}-1)+\beta^{96}(\beta^{12}-1)=2\cdot3^{24}\cdot26=52\times3^{24}\). Hence option (C).
authoredSolutions.47: \(Q=\tfrac12(A-A^\top)\) has \(\det Q=\tfrac{(3-a)^2}{4}=9\Rightarrow a=9\) or \(-3\). \(P=\tfrac12(A+A^\top)\) has \(\det P=-\tfrac{(3+a)^2}{4}\), giving \(-36\) (\(a{=}9\)) or \(0\) (\(a{=}-3\)). The modulus of their sum is \(|-36+0|=36\). Hence option (A).
authoredSolutions.48: Since \(|\bar z\omega|=1\) and \(\arg(\bar z\omega)=-(\arg z-\arg\omega)=-\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\equiv\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(\bar z\omega=i\). Then \(\dfrac{1-2i}{1+3i}=-\tfrac12-\tfrac12 i\), which lies in the third quadrant with argument \(-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\). Hence option (B). [Source key (C) is incorrect.]
authoredSolutions.49: \(\cos B=\tfrac35\Rightarrow\sin B=\tfrac45\); the sine rule gives \(b=2R\sin B=8\) and \(\sin C=\tfrac{AB}{2R}=\tfrac12\), so \(C=30^\circ\) and \(A=180^\circ-B-30^\circ\). Area \(=\tfrac12\,b\,c\,\sin A=\tfrac12\cdot8\cdot5\cdot\sin A=6+8\sqrt3\). Hence option (C).
authoredSolutions.50: Requiring the radicand \(\dfrac{||[x]|-2|}{|[x]|-3}\ge0\) (with denominator \(\neq0\)) and translating the resulting greatest-integer intervals back to \(x\) gives the domain \((-\infty,a)\cup[b,c)\cup[4,\infty)\) with \(a+b+c=-2\). Hence option (C).
authoredSolutions.51: Putting \(y=vx\) makes the equation separable; solving and applying \(y(\tfrac12)=\tfrac{\pi}{6}\) determines the curve \(y=y(x)\), and the area it bounds with \(x=0\) and \(x=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) in the upper half plane evaluates to \(\tfrac18(\pi-1)\). Hence option (A).
authoredSolutions.52: Because \((1-x)(x^2+x+1)=1-x^3\), the expression is \((1-x)(1-x^3)^{100}\). The \(x^{256}\) term comes only from \(-x\cdot(-1)^{85}\,{}^{100}C_{85}x^{255}\), giving coefficient \({}^{100}C_{85}={}^{100}C_{15}\). Hence option (B).

authoredSolutions.54: \(|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2-2(\vec a\cdot\vec c)+|\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2-2|\vec c|+9=8\Rightarrow|\vec c|=1\). With \(\vec a\times\vec b=(2,-2,1)\), \(|\vec a\times\vec b|=3\), so \(|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c|=|\vec a\times\vec b||\vec c|\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}=3\cdot1\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac32\). authoredSolutions.55: \(\sin^{-1}\sqrt{x^2+x+1}\) needs \(x^2+x\le0\) (\(x\in[-1,0]\)); \(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{x(x+1)}\) needs \(x(x+1)\ge0\) (\(x\le-1\) or \(x\ge0\)). The only common points are \(x=0,-1\), and at both the left side equals \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\neq\tfrac{\pi}{4}\). So there are no real roots. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.56: Multiplying through by \(x\) and separating, \(x e^x dx=-\dfrac{y\,dy}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}\), which integrates to \((x-1)e^x=\sqrt{1-y^2}+C\); applying the given conditions yields \((y(c))^2=1-4e^{6}\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.57: \(f\) increasing then decreasing about \(x=\tfrac34\) forces \(a<0\) with vertex \(-\tfrac{3}{a}=\tfrac34\Rightarrow a=-4\). Then \(g(x)=-4x^2-6x+15\) has \(g'(x)=-8x-6=0\) at \(x=-\tfrac34\) with \(g''<0\): a local maximum at \(x=-\tfrac34\). Hence option (A).
authoredSolutions.58: Continuity at \(x=0\): \(\sin0-e^0=-1\) must equal \(a+[-x]\to a-1\) (since \([-x]=-1\) for \(0<x<1\)), so \(a=0\). Continuity at \(x=1\): \(a-1=-1\) must equal \(2(1)-b\), so \(b=3\). Thus \(a+b=3\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.59: EXAMINATION has 11 letters with \(M\) appearing once. By symmetry every position is equally likely to hold the single \(M\), so \(P(M\text{ at 4th})=\tfrac1{11}\). Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.60: \(x^2+2(a+4)x-5a+64>0\) for all \(x\) needs discriminant \(<0\): \((a+4)^2-(-5a+64)<0\Rightarrow a^2+13a-48<0\Rightarrow -16<a<3\). Integers in \([-5,30]\) satisfying this are \(-5,\dots,2\) (8 values) out of 36, so the probability is \(\tfrac{8}{36}=\tfrac29\). Hence option (B).
